Do you switch out? Do you want to switch out? No, I'm good. Okay. You want to switch out? All right, just let me know. What's your mind? Just so you guys know, this is the cruiser bomb trap. What's for a pedestrian traffic or vehicle traffic pump? This incident occurred on December 7th, 2025 in Columbus, Ohio. Columbus police officer Caitlin Robinson was the responding officer involved in the crash. The driver of the white pickup truck, 30-year-old Corey Tennis, was rushed to the hospital in critical condition following the collision. However, less than 30 minutes later, he was pronounced dead at the hospital. Officer Robinson was also transported to a hospital, received treatment, and was later released in stable condition. An analysis of the dash cam footage reveals the approximate maximum speed of the officer during her response. This speed calculation shows the officer's estimated top speed during her entire response. The prior speed calculation shown earlier is her estimated speed the moment she collided with the truck. The truck the victim was driving was an early 2000 Chevy Silverado. I-IHS safety ratings show that its overall rating is marginal, meaning it's acceptable but not good. Furthermore, when looking at the specific ratings of the truck's structure and safety cage as well as driver movement during a crash, those categories were both given poor ratings by the IHS. Not surprisingly, this resulted in the truck being destroyed, and early indicators suggest the driver was also not wearing his seatbelt, resulting in him being ejected from the vehicle. The obituary of the driver, who tragically lost his life, Corey states he was a loving son, father, fiancé, brother, and uncle. If you would like to donate to Corey's GoFundMe page set up by his family, a link can be found in the description below. In Columbus, these cops were responding to an officer's shot, but they would never make the scene in order to help their partner. Instead, they would need their own emergency response. In Seattle, this officer was responding to a medical but only chirped his siren then responded lights only. He fatally struck a college student wearing her AirPods. There's no reason to respond lights only to a medical. Then in LA, this officer was responding light to sirens and driving down the center lane when he fatally struck a skateboarder. Whenever half a second he saved by driving in the middle lane was surely not worth it. All told, these are entirely avoidable incidents and deaths, and the fact that they are so avoidable makes the tragedy all the worst. In Columbus, Ohio, with his body cam footage originates, proper procedure when officers use emergency vehicle operations or EVO is described in the Columbus Police Division Directive. It states that going through red light intersections while using EVO poses a heightened level of risk and requires an increased level of cost. Therefore, sworn personnel shall slow down as necessary for the safety of traffic and shall proceed into these intersections at a speed which will allow sworn personnel and or other drivers and pedestrians a reasonable opportunity to avoid a traffic crash. Proper procedure among all United States police departments is this. If you cannot safely clear an intersection, you do not go no matter how urgent the call is. You can follow policy and still be brave, but you can't ignore policy and call it courage because the job is to arrive ready to help, not to become the next call over the radio.
